summary: Gives guidelines for designers using UDP, focusing on congestion control but also covering message size, reliability, checksums and middleboxes. It is a BCP.

plainLanguage.summary: UDP leaves important delivery decisions to the application. This Best Current Practice explains how designers should control traffic, choose message sizes, handle loss, and protect communication.

subtitle: Design guidance for using UDP safely, with congestion control as the central requirement.

tldr.problem: UDP provides no inherent congestion control, reliability, ordering, or path-size discovery, leaving applications responsible for those behaviors.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends controlling sending rates, limiting message sizes, handling loss and duplicates, enabling checksums, and accounting for middleboxes and security.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8085 is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 5405 and has been updated by RFC 8899.

today: RFC 8085 is Best Current Practice BCP 145. It obsoletes RFC 5405 and has been updated by RFC 8899.

sections.title: Why UDP Needs Usage Guidelines
sections.content:
UDP provides a minimal, unreliable, best-effort message transport over IP. It creates no end-to-end connection and keeps little state, but it also provides no inherent congestion control. An application can send at its interface's line rate, which may exceed what the path can carry.

Applications using UDP on the Internet must prevent congestion collapse and support fair sharing with other traffic. The RFC recommends using an existing IETF transport when its features meet the application's needs. It covers unicast, multicast, broadcast, anycast, and tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP sends messages without controlling how quickly they enter the network. Applications must manage that rate so they do not overwhelm a shared path.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Sending Rates
sections.content:
An application that chooses UDP SHOULD control its sending rate to each destination across all its sockets and processes. Bulk transfers SHOULD use TFRC, TCP-like window control, or another method that competes fairly with TCP within an order of magnitude.

Low-volume applications SHOULD send no more than one datagram per round-trip time on average. If they cannot estimate round-trip time, the RFC recommends an initial interval of 1 second; applications with no return traffic SHOULD NOT send more than one datagram every 3 seconds. Senders SHOULD pace bursts, and a loss-detection timer MUST be treated as a congestion signal.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP applications should slow down when the network signals congestion. The appropriate sending rate depends on whether the application sends a large transfer or only occasional messages.

sections.title: ECN, Service Markings and Circuit Breakers
sections.content:
UDP applications may use Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), but they must negotiate compatible feedback, inspect each received datagram's ECN field, report congestion marks, and reduce the sending rate appropriately. Applications should not rely on a particular Differentiated Services Code Point receiving a specific treatment along the path.

Some controlled environments reserve network capacity and may choose not to use congestion control. For Internet traffic that lacks congestion control, the RFC recommends a circuit breaker: an automatic mechanism that stops or sharply reduces a flow when it detects excessive congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: ECN helps only when both endpoints report and respond to congestion marks. A circuit breaker can stop a flow when it causes excessive congestion.

sections.title: UDP Tunnels and Multicast
sections.content:
A UDP tunnel carries another protocol's packets inside UDP datagrams. If it carries congestion-controlled IP traffic at a matching volume, the tunnel SHOULD NOT add a separate congestion controller because the original senders already respond to congestion. A circuit breaker may still help control the aggregate traffic.

A tunnel carrying non-IP or uncontrolled traffic SHOULD use congestion control or a circuit breaker. A tunnel whose UDP rate does not track its payload needs additional analysis. Multicast applications SHOULD also provide congestion control that accounts for receivers with different path conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel should account for the traffic inside it. If the inner traffic already controls its rate, extra control may be unnecessary; otherwise, the tunnel needs its own safeguards.

sections.title: Datagram Size and Fragmentation
sections.content:
IP fragmentation lowers efficiency and reliability, and some NATs and firewalls drop fragments. Applications SHOULD avoid UDP datagrams that produce IP packets larger than the path MTU. They SHOULD use path MTU information or discovery; if they cannot, they SHOULD stay below the default effective sending MTU.

The RFC gives 576 bytes for IPv4, or the first-hop MTU if smaller, and 1280 bytes for IPv6 as default effective sending MTUs. To calculate the UDP payload size from an MTU, subtract the IP header, including options or extension headers, and the 8-byte UDP header.
sections.plainLanguage: Large packets may be split into fragments, and losing one fragment loses the whole packet. Applications should choose a datagram size that fits the path.

sections.title: Reliability, Ordering and Checksums
sections.content:
UDP does not retransmit lost datagrams, remove duplicates, or preserve order. Applications that need reliable or ordered delivery MUST provide those features themselves. They SHOULD handle delayed or duplicate packets within a 2-minute interval, and retransmissions must also follow congestion-control guidelines.

Applications SHOULD enable the UDP checksum. It checks the packet but is not strong protection against malicious changes, so important data may need an additional CRC or cryptographic hash. The checksum MUST be used over IPv6 except for tunnel protocols that meet the specified zero-checksum requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP does not guarantee that messages arrive once or in order. Applications must add those features when they need them and should check received data for errors.

sections.title: Middleboxes, Ports and Keepalives
sections.content:
NATs and firewalls may remove UDP flow state after a period without traffic, then drop later return packets. Applications SHOULD recover by re-establishing their sessions. Keepalives are not recommended for general use; when needed, they SHOULD be sent no more frequently than once every 15 seconds, with slight timing variation.

Senders SHOULD use randomized source ports and SHOULD NOT use source port zero. Tunnels using source ports for load-balancing entropy SHOULD use the ephemeral range 49152 to 65535 and SHOULD NOT change a flow's source port more than once every 30 seconds. Applications MUST NOT assume that middleboxes behave consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT or firewall may forget an inactive UDP flow, so an application needs a way to recover. If it uses keepalives, they should not be sent too often.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
UDP does not provide communication security. Applications that need confidentiality, integrity, or protection from forged messages SHOULD use end-to-end security from another IETF protocol. The RFC recommends established mechanisms such as DTLS or IPsec rather than inventing new ones.

Applications that send large responses to short requests can be abused for amplification attacks. They SHOULD limit this risk, for example by authenticating the sender or limiting the requests they answer. A source IP address alone is not an authenticator because it can be spoofed.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP does not protect private messages or prove who sent them. Applications need a separate security mechanism and should limit responses that could amplify attacks.
